\chapter{The Leg and the Tooth}
\label{ch:ml-body-more}
\hlchaptermodality{47}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name five more parts of the body in Malayalam, and point to the sound exchanges that separate them from their Tamil, Telugu and Kannada cousins.}

Complete ML-C47-stomach and say all five words in order.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[kāl]{\ml{കാൽ} (kāl) — leg, foot}

\label{lesson:ML-C47-leg}



\begin{quote}
Before the new run of words: what did \emph{uppŭ} mean, and what did \emph{pustakaṁ} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ml{കാൽ}}
\textbf{\ml{കാൽ}} (\emph{kāl}) — \textquotedblleft{}leg, foot\textquotedblright{}.

Proto-Dravidian \textbf{*kāl}, and every sister kept it nearly whole: Tamil \ta{கால்}, Telugu \te{కాలు}, Kannada \ka{ಕಾಲು}. Malayalam alone stops the word dead on its \emph{l}.

That final \ml{ൽ} is a chillu — a consonant written with no vowel after it and no virama under it, given a letter of its own. This book has already taught one of them, the \ml{ൾ} inside \ml{നിങ്ങൾ}. \ml{ൽ} is its plainer neighbour.

\ml{കാൽ} covers the whole limb, foot and leg together. It also names a quarter — a fourth of anything — so a quarter of a rupee and the leg you stand on are written the same way. Nothing joins them but an accident of sound, and context is the only fix, which is what context is for.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The first of five more body words.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{kāl}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{kāl}, then \emph{kaṇṇŭ}, so the bottom and the top sit together
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ml{കാൽ} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}leg, foot\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[pallŭ]{\ml{പല്ല്} (pallŭ) — a tooth}

\label{lesson:ML-C47-tooth}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{kāl} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ml{പല്ല്}}
\textbf{\ml{പല്ല്}} (\emph{pallŭ}) — \textquotedblleft{}a tooth\textquotedblright{}.

Proto-Dravidian \textbf{*pal}, another word the family barely touched: Tamil \ta{பல்}, Telugu \te{పన్ను}, Kannada \ka{ಹಲ್ಲು}.

Kannada is the odd one again, and for the reason already met with the fruit — an opening \emph{p} that became \emph{h}. Set \ka{ಹಲ್ಲು} beside \ml{പല്ല്} and the only real difference is that first letter. Telugu did something else altogether, turning the \emph{l} into an \emph{n}.

Malayalam doubles the \emph{l} and then lets the word go with the half-vowel, the same ending as the salt-word.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Two body words: a leg and a tooth.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{pallŭ}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{kāl}, then \emph{pallŭ}, and hear the doubled letter in the second
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ml{പല്ല്} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a tooth\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[muṭi]{\ml{മുടി} (muṭi) — hair}

\label{lesson:ML-C47-hair}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{pallŭ} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ml{മുടി}}
\textbf{\ml{മുടി}} (\emph{muṭi}) — \textquotedblleft{}hair\textquotedblright{}.

The everyday word for the hair on a head. Tamil \ta{முடி} (\emph{muṭi}) is the same word, and in both languages it keeps company with a sense of finishing or topping off — the crown of a thing as well as what grows there.

Kannada took a different route entirely, \ka{ಕೂದಲು} (\emph{kūdalu}), which Tamil also has as \ta{கூந்தல்} (\emph{kūntal}) for long hair worn loose. So the family has two hair-words and the sisters split over which one became the ordinary one.

Malayalam keeps \ml{രോമം} (\emph{rōmaṁ}), a Sanskrit word, for hair on the body rather than the head — a second case of a borrowing taking the narrower job.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Three. A leg, a tooth, hair.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{muṭi}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{muṭi}, then \emph{thala}, so the head and what grows on it sit together
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ml{മുടി} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}hair\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[viral]{\ml{വിരൽ} (viral) — a finger}

\label{lesson:ML-C47-finger}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{muṭi} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ml{വിരൽ}}
\textbf{\ml{വിരൽ}} (\emph{viral}) — \textquotedblleft{}a finger\textquotedblright{}.

Proto-Dravidian \textbf{*viral}, and Tamil \ta{விரல்} (\emph{viral}) matches Malayalam letter for letter, chillu and all.

Kannada has \ka{ಬೆರಳು} (\emph{beraḷu}), where the opening \emph{v-} has hardened into a \emph{b-}. That exchange runs the other way through the family often enough to be worth naming: a \emph{v} at the front of a Kannada word is frequently a \emph{b}, and this is one of the clearest cases. Telugu walked away from the root and says \te{వేలు} (\emph{vēlu}).

The word ends in the same chillu \ml{ൽ} as the leg-word, two chapters' worth of body parts stopping on the same letter.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Four. A leg, a tooth, hair, a finger.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{viral}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{viral}, then \emph{kāl}, and hear the same chillu close both
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ml{വിരൽ} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a finger\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[vayaṟŭ]{\ml{വയറ്} (vayaṟŭ) — the stomach, the belly}

\label{lesson:ML-C47-stomach}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{viral} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ml{വയറ്}}
\textbf{\ml{വയറ്}} (\emph{vayaṟŭ}) — \textquotedblleft{}the stomach, the belly\textquotedblright{}.

Native, and Tamil \ta{வயிறு} (\emph{vayiṟu}) is again the near-twin. The two sisters agree on the belly where the other two do not: Kannada says \ka{ಹೊಟ್ಟೆ} (\emph{hoṭṭe}) and Telugu \te{పొట్ట} (\emph{poṭṭa}), a pair that plainly belong together and just as plainly do not belong with this one.

So on a single body the family sorts itself twice over. Leg, tooth and finger run back to one shared ancestor; the belly splits the four into two camps of two.

The ends of these words are worth a moment as well. This one closes on \ml{റ്} , the hard \emph{ṟ} with the half-vowel after it.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five, and the run is closed: a leg, a tooth, hair, a finger, a belly.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{vayaṟŭ}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item all five in order — \emph{kāl}, \emph{pallŭ}, \emph{muṭi}, \emph{viral}, \emph{vayaṟŭ}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ml{വയറ്} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}the stomach, the belly\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
